focus.text: When one verb follows another, the second verb changes shape. Some verbs are followed by an *-ing* form (*enjoy writing*), some by *to* + base verb (*decide to write*), and a few by either. After a preposition, English always uses the *-ing* form, which is why *look forward to hearing* is correct. Some verbs need an object first (*ask somebody to help*), and a small group — *make, let, have* — take an object and then a bare base verb. Choosing the wrong pattern is one of the errors a reader notices first.

summaryTable.caption: Four patterns after a verb
rows: They **decided to move** to Đà Nẵng.
My tutor **advised me to rewrite** the introduction.

pretest.sentence: Hoa enjoys cooking for her whole family at the weekend.
pretest.reason: *enjoy* is always followed by the *-ing* form.

pretest.sentence: My teacher suggested me to join the debate club.
pretest.reason: *suggest* is not followed by object + infinitive: *suggested that I join* or *suggested joining*.

pretest.sentence: We have decided to move the meeting to Thursday.
I look forward to hear from you soon.
pretest.reason: The *to* in *look forward to* is a preposition, so the verb takes *-ing*: *hearing*.

pretest.sentence: This app makes me to study for twenty minutes every day.
pretest.reason: *make* + object + base verb, with no *to*: *makes me study*.

pretest.sentence: She is good at explaining difficult ideas to younger students.
pretest.reason: After the preposition *at*, the verb takes the *-ing* form.

pretest.sentence: My parents want that I study medicine.
pretest.reason: *want* takes an object and then an infinitive: *want me to study*.

pretest.sentence: I remember visiting that pagoda when I was seven.
pretest.reason: *remember* + *-ing* is the memory of something that already happened.

pretest.sentence: I am used to get up at five o'clock now.
pretest.reason: *be used to* means 'accustomed to', so it takes the *-ing* form: *used to getting up*.

pretest.sentence: He stopped to buy a bottle of water on the way home.
pretest.reason: *stop* + *to* + base verb means he paused in order to do something.

context.title: Finding a place to study
context.paragraph: Since she started university, Trang has tried studying in three different places. She avoids working at home, because her younger brother keeps asking her questions. Last term she decided to book a desk in the university library, but by March she could not afford to renew it. Her flatmate suggested using the café below their building, and Trang agreed to give it a try. She is now used to writing with music in the background, although she still refuses to study after midnight. Her tutor has encouraged her to plan each week on Sunday evening, and that small habit has made her feel much calmer about deadlines.

sections.title: Forming the -ing form and the infinitive

table.caption: The two forms, positive and negative
rows: He **promised not to be** late again.

notes: Spelling of the *-ing* form: drop a silent -e (*make → making*), double a final consonant after one stressed vowel (*begin → beginning*), and change -ie to -y (*lie → lying*).

items.stem: Minh finished ___ his essay just before midnight.
items.reason: *finish* is always followed by the *-ing* form.

items.stem: We cannot afford ___ a new printer this term.
Thank you for ___ me with the poster.
items.reason: After a preposition (*for*), the verb takes the *-ing* form.

items.stem: Her parents let her ___ to Hà Nội alone.
The teacher advised us ___ the introduction last.
items.reason: *advise* takes an object and then *to* + base verb.

sections.title: Using verbs followed by -ing or by to

rules.text: Verbs about liking, avoiding and continuing usually take the *-ing* form: *enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, practise, mind, suggest, consider*.

examples.text: Nam **avoids taking** the ring road at rush hour.
I **suggest starting** with the cheapest option.

rules.text: Verbs about plans, wishes and decisions usually take *to* + base verb: *decide, hope, plan, want, agree, refuse, learn, manage, afford*.

examples.text: The committee **agreed to publish** the results in June.
She **managed to finish** the course while working part time.

rules.text: After a preposition, always use the *-ing* form. This includes the *to* in *look forward to*, *be used to* and *object to*.

examples.text: Huy is interested **in volunteering** at the animal shelter.
We look forward **to meeting** you in September.

tips: Test a *to* before you write. If a noun can follow it (*look forward to the holiday*), it is a preposition and the verb takes *-ing*. If a noun cannot, it is an infinitive.

items.stem: She has promised ___ us before the deadline.
I am looking forward to ___ my cousins in Cần Thơ.
items.reason: The *to* in *look forward to* is a preposition, so the verb takes *-ing*.

items.stem: The heavy rain made the road ___ dangerous.
My coach encouraged me ___ for the regional team.
items.reason: *encourage* takes an object and then *to* + base verb.

sections.title: Forming patterns with an object

table.caption: Verbs that need an object before the second verb
rows: ask, tell, advise, encourage, allow, remind, want, expect
The school **allowed us to leave** early.
Her parents **let her stay** with friends.
She **suggested that we meet** at eight.

notes: *Suggest* and *recommend* never take an object + infinitive. Write *suggest doing something*, *suggest that somebody do something*, or *recommend a place*, but never *suggest me to do*.

items.sentence: My teacher suggested me to read one article a day.
items.reason: *suggest* is not followed by object + infinitive.

items.sentence: Loud music makes me to lose concentration.
I am looking forward to receive your reply.
items.reason: The *to* in *look forward to* is a preposition, so the verb takes *-ing*.

items.sentence: She is used to work night shifts at the hotel.
items.reason: *be used to* means 'accustomed to', so it is followed by the *-ing* form.

items.sentence: They want that their son studies abroad.
items.reason: *want* takes an object and an infinitive, not a *that*-clause.

sections.title: Using verbs that change meaning

rules.text: *Stop*, *remember*, *forget* and *regret* change meaning with each form. The *-ing* form looks back at something that already happened; *to* + base verb looks forward to the action.

examples.text: He **stopped buying** bottled water, so he carries a flask now.
He **stopped to buy** water on the way to the station.
I **remember locking** the gate, but please check it again.

rules.text: *Try* + *-ing* means experiment with a different method; *try* + *to* means make an effort at something difficult.

examples.text: **Try writing** your plan on paper before you open the laptop.
She **tried to finish** the whole paper in one evening.

rules.text: Keep *used to* and *be used to* apart: *used to* + base verb is a habit that has stopped, while *be* or *get used to* + *-ing* is becoming accustomed to something.

examples.text: We **used to live** near the river before the flood.
I **am getting used to cycling** in the rain.

notes: *Remember to send the file* is a task you must not forget; *remember sending the file* is the memory of having sent it. In instructions you almost always want the infinitive.
tips: In an email, *I regret to inform you* announces bad news now, while *I regret telling him* looks back with sorrow. Read both aloud before you choose one.

editing.text: Last year I decided improving my English before the university entrance exam. My cousin suggested me to keep a diary in English, so I started writing one every evening. At first I avoided to write about difficult topics, because I was afraid of make mistakes. After a month I got used to write about anything, and I stopped worrying about grammar. My teacher encouraged me to read my diary aloud, which made me to notice the errors myself. I also tried recording my voice, and now I enjoy listening to those first recordings. They are funny, but they show real progress. I remember to write a whole page about my grandmother's garden in Huế; that page still makes me smile. This year I want that my sister starts a diary too, because she work very hard but she never practises writing.

errors.reason: *suggest* is not followed by object + infinitive.
After the preposition *of*, the verb takes the *-ing* form.
*get used to* means 'become accustomed to', so it takes the *-ing* form.

errors.span: remember to write a whole page
errors.reason: The memory of a past action takes the *-ing* form.
*want* takes an object and an infinitive, not a *that*-clause.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a language exchange partner you have not met yet. Explain why you want to practise with them, what you enjoy doing in English, and what you would like to work on this year.
checklist: At least three verbs are followed by an *-ing* form and three by *to* + base verb.
The email closes politely with *look forward to* + *-ing*.

topics.prompt: "Students should be allowed to choose all of their own subjects at seventeen." Give your view and support it with reasons.
checklist: *allow, let, make* and *encourage* each appear with the right pattern after the object.
At least two verbs of decision take *to* + base verb (*decide, refuse, agree*).
*suggest* and *recommend* are never followed by an object + infinitive.

topics.prompt: Describe a habit you have changed: getting up earlier, spending less time on your phone, or cycling to school. Say what you used to do, what you have got used to, and what you have stopped doing.
checklist: *used to* + base verb describes the old habit.
*be* or *get used to* + *-ing* describes the new one.
At least one sentence uses *stop*, *remember* or *try* with the form that matches your meaning.
